Serverless and Event-Driven Foundations and AWS Lambda

Build serverless, event-driven applications with AWS Lambda: foundations, invocation, concurrency, security, edge functions, and cost.

Overview and Objectives

Lesson Overview

Serverless, Integration, and Event-Driven Design

Module 273, Serverless, Integration, and Event-Driven Design, covers serverless compute, application integration, and event-driven architectures on AWS. This lesson starts with the foundations and AWS Lambda, the core serverless compute service.

Serverless applications run code without servers to manage, scale with each request, and cost nothing while idle. This lesson explains serverless and event-driven foundations, and then AWS Lambda in depth: how functions run, how they are invoked, how they scale, how they are secured and connected to a VPC, how they run at the edge, and what they cost. The last two tabs prepare you for the AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate (SAA-C03) exam.

The tabs in this lesson cover the following topics:

  • Tab 1: serverless computing, AWS serverless services, and when serverless fits.
  • Tab 2: synchronous and asynchronous communication, loose coupling, event-driven architecture, and choreography compared with orchestration.
  • Tab 3: Lambda functions, runtimes, the execution environment, limits, layers, versions, and aliases.
  • Tab 4: synchronous, asynchronous, and event source mapping invocations, error handling, patterns, and function URLs.
  • Tab 5: concurrency, reserved and provisioned concurrency, cold starts, SnapStart, and tuning.
  • Tab 6: execution roles, VPC access, RDS Proxy, Lambda with Amazon EFS, and monitoring.
  • Tab 7: CloudFront Functions, Lambda@Edge and its triggers and restrictions, and newer Lambda options.
  • Tab 8: what you pay for and how to lower the cost.
  • Tab 9: compute and messaging comparisons, and the SAA-C03 cheat sheet.
  • Tab 10: open-ended Knowledge Check questions with model answers.

Introduction

Many applications have traffic that rises and falls sharply: a flash sale, a file upload, a scheduled report. Servers sized for the peak sit idle most of the time, and servers sized for the average fail at the peak. Serverless, event-driven designs run code only when something happens and scale with it, and AWS Lambda is at their center.

This lesson follows FlashCart Inc. through the Problem Statement of each tab. It assumes that you know Amazon EC2, VPC networking, and the database services from Module 272. It opens Module 273.

Use the tab list on the left, or the Previous and Next buttons, to move through the lesson. Each topic tab opens with a Problem Statement and ends with exam traps, keyword triggers, and resource links. The Knowledge Check is the last tab.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, learners will be able to:

  1. Define serverless computing and identify AWS serverless services.
  2. Explain synchronous and asynchronous communication, loose coupling, and event-driven architectures.
  3. Describe AWS Lambda functions, the execution environment, packaging, and limits.
  4. Use the synchronous, asynchronous, and event source mapping invocation types and their error handling.
  5. Compare reserved concurrency, provisioned concurrency, and SnapStart for scaling and performance.
  6. Apply IAM, VPC, RDS Proxy, and monitoring features to secure and operate Lambda functions.
  7. Design a cost-effective, event-driven serverless solution with AWS Lambda.

1. Serverless Foundations

Problem Statement

FlashCart runs its order API on a fleet of EC2 instances. Traffic is low at night and spikes ten times during flash sales, so the team pays for idle servers most of the day and still scrambles to add capacity before each sale. The architects ask whether a serverless design would remove the servers to manage and match the cost to the real traffic.

1.1 What Serverless Means

  • Serverless is a way to build applications where you do not provision, patch, or manage servers. You deploy code, functions, or configuration, and AWS runs it.
  • Serverless does not mean there are no servers. It means that you do not manage, provision, or see them.
  • It started as Function as a Service (FaaS) with AWS Lambda, and it now includes any fully managed service: databases, messaging, storage, and more.
  • A serverless service usually has four traits: no server management, automatic scaling, pay for value (you pay for use, not for idle capacity), and built-in high availability.

1.2 Serverless Services on AWS

NeedServerless service
Run codeAWS Lambda, and AWS Fargate for containers.
Expose an APIAmazon API Gateway, and Lambda function URLs.
Messaging and eventsAmazon SQS (queues), Amazon SNS (pub/sub), and Amazon EventBridge (event bus).
Orchestrate stepsAWS Step Functions.
Store dataAmazon DynamoDB, Amazon S3, and Aurora Serverless v2.
Stream dataKinesis Data Streams and Amazon Data Firehose.
Sign in usersAmazon Cognito.

1.3 Serverless Compared With Servers

Amazon EC2 (servers)Serverless (Lambda)
What you manageThe operating system, patches, scaling, and capacity.Only the code and its configuration.
Running timeContinuously running.Runs on demand, for short executions (up to 15 minutes).
ScalingYou add or remove instances, or set up Auto Scaling.Automatic, per request or message.
Cost when idleYou pay while the instance runs.No requests, no compute charge.
LimitsRAM and CPU of the instance.Execution time, memory, and payload size.

1.4 When Serverless Is Not the Best Fit

  • Work that runs longer than 15 minutes in one invocation, such as a long batch job. Use AWS Batch, ECS, EC2, or Step Functions to split the work.
  • Steady, heavy traffic all day, where a reserved server can cost less than paying per request.
  • Software that needs full control of the operating system, special hardware, or a long-lived local state.
  • Very low-latency workloads that cannot accept a cold start, unless you use provisioned concurrency or SnapStart (tab 5).

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A company has an internal reporting API that receives a few hundred requests a day, with long idle periods. The team wants to stop patching servers and pay only when the API is used. What should a solutions architect recommend?

  • A. Amazon API Gateway with AWS Lambda.
  • B. Two EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer.
  • C. An EC2 Reserved Instance.
  • D. A container cluster on Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: A. API Gateway and Lambda are serverless: no servers to patch, automatic scaling, and no compute charge while the API is idle.

OptionResultReason
ACorrectIt matches the low, spiky traffic and the pay-for-use goal.
BIncorrectThe instances run and cost money all day, and the team still patches them.
CIncorrectA reservation lowers the price of a server that is mostly idle.
DIncorrectA cluster still needs servers and capacity management.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • Serverless does not mean no servers. It means that you do not manage them.
  • Serverless is not only Lambda: DynamoDB, S3, SQS, SNS, API Gateway, Step Functions, and Fargate are serverless too.
  • A task longer than 15 minutes is not a single Lambda invocation.

Memory Hook

No servers to manage, scale on demand, pay for use, available by default.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "No servers to manage, pay only when used, automatic scaling"
→ A serverless design (Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB)

Trigger 2: "Run containers without managing servers"
→ AWS Fargate

Trigger 3: "Job longer than 15 minutes"
→ Not a single Lambda: use Batch, ECS, EC2, or Step Functions

2. Event-Driven Architecture

Problem Statement

When a FlashCart customer places an order, the order API calls the payment service, the email service, and the analytics service one after another. If the email service is slow, the customer waits. If it fails, the whole order fails. During a flash sale, the analytics service cannot keep up and slows everything down.

2.1 Synchronous and Asynchronous Communication

  • In synchronous communication, the caller sends a request and waits for the answer, like a phone call. If the receiver is slow or down, the caller is slow or fails too.
  • In asynchronous communication, the caller sends a message and moves on, like a text message. The receiver processes it when it can.
  • Synchronous calls between services are a problem when traffic spikes suddenly. For example, the system usually encodes 10 videos, but suddenly must encode 1,000.

2.2 Loose Coupling

  • Modern applications rely on many services working together, and the way they communicate decides how reliable and scalable the system is.
  • Loosely coupled systems communicate asynchronously through a service in the middle. They:
  • Allow each service to scale independently.
  • Absorb sudden traffic spikes in a queue or stream.
  • Prevent a failure in one service from breaking the others.
  • Let you add a new consumer without changing the producer.
Decoupling modelAWS serviceHow it works
QueueAmazon SQSProducers put messages in a queue, and consumers pull and process them at their own pace.
Publish/subscribeAmazon SNSOne message is pushed to many subscribers at the same time.
Event busAmazon EventBridgeEvents are routed by rules to many targets, including SaaS and AWS service events.
Real-time streamAmazon Kinesis Data StreamsOrdered records are kept for a time and read by many consumers.

2.3 Event-Driven Architecture

  • An event is a change in state, such as "order placed", "file uploaded", or "temperature above 30 degrees".
  • In an event-driven architecture, producers publish events, a router filters and delivers them, and consumers react to them.
  • Producers do not know who consumes their events, so new consumers can be added without changing the producers.
  • AWS Lambda is a natural consumer: it runs only when an event arrives.

2.4 Choreography and Orchestration

ChoreographyOrchestration
How it worksEach service reacts to events and publishes new ones. No service is in charge.A central workflow calls each step in order and handles the errors.
AWS exampleAmazon EventBridge or SNS with Lambda consumers.AWS Step Functions.
Use it whenServices are independent and new reactions are added often.Steps must run in order, with retries, branches, and a clear status.

2.5 Example: A Serverless Voting App

  • In the real-time (synchronous) version, API Gateway invokes the GetVote, UpdateVote, and DeleteVote functions directly, and they write to DynamoDB.
  • In the event-based (asynchronous) version, a buffer (a queue) sits between API Gateway and the update functions, so a spike of votes waits in the queue instead of overloading the functions and the database.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: An order service calls the email, analytics, and loyalty services directly, one after another. When one of them is slow, orders are delayed. The company wants each service to process orders independently and to add new services later without changing the order service. What should a solutions architect recommend?

  • A. Call the three services in parallel threads in the order service.
  • B. Add more EC2 instances to the order service.
  • C. Publish an "order placed" event to Amazon EventBridge or SNS, and let each service consume it.
  • D. Store the orders in a larger database instance.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: C. Publishing events decouples the producer from the consumers: each consumer scales and fails on its own, and new consumers subscribe without changes to the order service.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectParallel calls are still synchronous and tightly coupled.
BIncorrectMore instances do not remove the dependency on slow services.
CCorrectThis is an event-driven, loosely coupled design.
DIncorrectThe database is not the bottleneck.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • Decouple, absorb spikes, independent scaling point to SQS, SNS, EventBridge, or Kinesis.
  • Fan-out of one message to many consumers = SNS (often SNS plus SQS). Buffer work for consumers = SQS.
  • Ordered steps with retries and status = Step Functions (orchestration), not a chain of Lambda functions calling each other.

Memory Hook

Phone call = synchronous and coupled. Text message = asynchronous and decoupled.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Decouple services and absorb traffic spikes"
→ Amazon SQS

Trigger 2: "One event to many subscribers"
→ Amazon SNS or Amazon EventBridge

Trigger 3: "Route events by rules, including SaaS events"
→ Amazon EventBridge

Trigger 4: "Coordinate ordered steps with retries"
→ AWS Step Functions

3. What AWS Lambda Is

Problem Statement

The FlashCart team decides to move the order API to AWS Lambda. Before they write code, they need to understand what a Lambda function is, how it runs, which languages and packages it accepts, and which limits they must design around.

3.1 What AWS Lambda Is

  • AWS Lambda is a serverless, event-driven compute service that runs your code as functions, without servers to provision or manage.
  • It is ideal for stateless execution: each invocation must not depend on data kept in memory from a previous one.
  • It scales automatically with the number of requests or messages.
  • You write a function, or upload a package with the code and its dependencies.
  • It is triggered by more than 50 event sources, such as API Gateway, EventBridge, SQS, Kinesis, S3, and DynamoDB Streams.
  • It uses an IAM execution role to access other AWS services, such as S3 and DynamoDB.
  • It sends logs and metrics to Amazon CloudWatch.

3.2 Functions, Handlers, and Runtimes

  • The handler is the method in your code that Lambda calls with each event. It receives the event and a context object.
  • Lambda offers managed runtimes for Node.js, Python, Java, .NET, and Ruby. Other languages, such as Go and Rust, run on an OS-only runtime with the Runtime API.
  • You can package a function as a .zip file archive or as a container image. A container image must implement the Lambda Runtime API. For arbitrary Docker images, ECS or Fargate is preferred.
  • You can choose the x86_64 or the arm64 (AWS Graviton) architecture.
import json

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    order_id = event.get("orderId")
    # process the order here
    return {"statusCode": 200, "body": json.dumps({"orderId": order_id, "status": "accepted"})}

3.3 The Execution Environment

  • Lambda runs each function in a secure, isolated execution environment.
  • In the Init phase, Lambda downloads the code, starts the runtime, and runs the code outside the handler. In the Invoke phase, it runs the handler for an event.
  • A cold start is an invocation that needs a new environment, so it includes the Init phase. A warm environment is reused for later events.
  • Put the setup work, such as SDK clients and database connections, outside the handler, so that warm invocations reuse it.
  • Each environment has a /tmp directory for temporary files.

3.4 Configuration and Limits

SettingLimit
Memory128 MB to 10,240 MB, in 1 MB steps. CPU grows with memory: at 1,769 MB, a function has the equivalent of one vCPU.
TimeoutUp to 900 seconds (15 minutes).
Environment variables4 KB in total for a function.
LayersUp to 5 layers per function.
/tmp storage512 MB to 10,240 MB.
Deployment package (.zip)50 MB zipped when uploaded directly (upload larger files with S3), and 250 MB unzipped, including layers.
Container imageUp to 10 GB, uncompressed.
Invocation payload6 MB for a synchronous request and for its response, and 1 MB for an asynchronous request. A streamed response can be up to 200 MB.
Concurrent executions1,000 per Region by default, shared by all functions, and it can be increased. New accounts start lower.

3.5 Layers, Versions, and Aliases

  • A layer is a .zip archive of shared code or libraries that several functions can use.
  • A version is an immutable snapshot of the function code and configuration. $LATEST is the most recent, unpublished code.
  • An alias is a named pointer, such as dev, test, or prod, to a version. Clients call the alias, so you can switch versions without changing the clients.
  • An alias can split traffic between two versions with weights, for example 80 percent to version 3 and 20 percent to version 4, for a canary release.
  • Do not use $LATEST in production. Use published versions and aliases for reliable releases and quick rollback.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A data team must run a nightly job that transforms files for about 40 minutes. A developer suggests one Lambda function with the maximum timeout. What should a solutions architect say?

  • A. Set the Lambda timeout to 60 minutes.
  • B. Lambda cannot run one invocation longer than 15 minutes, so use AWS Batch, ECS, or split the work into smaller steps.
  • C. Increase the memory to 10,240 MB so the timeout is extended.
  • D. Use a Lambda layer to extend the timeout.

OptionResultReason

4. Invoking Lambda

Problem Statement

FlashCart needs three things from Lambda: answer API calls from the website, create a thumbnail when a product image is uploaded to S3, and process order messages from an SQS queue. The team must understand how Lambda is invoked in each case, and what happens when an invocation fails.

4.1 The Three Ways to Invoke Lambda

TypeHow it worksExamplesOn error
SynchronousThe caller waits for the function to finish and gets the response.API Gateway, Application Load Balancer, Lambda function URLs, and the SDK or CLI.The caller gets the error and decides whether to retry. On throttling, it gets a 429 TooManyRequestsException.
AsynchronousLambda queues the event internally and returns at once. The function runs later.S3 event notifications, SNS, and EventBridge.Lambda retries 2 more times, then sends the event to a dead-letter queue or an on-failure destination.
Event source mappingLambda polls a queue or stream and invokes the function with batches of records.SQS, Kinesis Data Streams, DynamoDB Streams, Amazon MSK, and Amazon MQ.Depends on the source: for SQS, failed messages return to the queue; for streams, Lambda retries the batch.

4.2 Asynchronous Invocation in Detail

  • On a function error, Lambda retries the event 2 more times.
  • On throttling (429) or a system error (500-series), Lambda returns the event to its internal queue and keeps retrying for up to 6 hours, with intervals that grow from 1 second to 5 minutes.
  • After all the retries, Lambda sends the event to a dead-letter queue (SQS or SNS), or to an on-failure destination.
  • Destinations can send the result of a success or a failure to SQS, SNS, EventBridge, or another Lambda function.

4.3 Common Patterns

PatternHow it works
API backendAPI Gateway or an Application Load Balancer invokes Lambda on each request.
Message processingLambda reads SQS messages as they arrive in the queue, often after SNS fan-out.
S3 event processingAn object upload to S3 triggers Lambda, for example to create a thumbnail.
Real-time stream processingLambda reads records from Kinesis Data Streams or DynamoDB Streams.
Scheduled tasksAn EventBridge rule or schedule runs Lambda, like a serverless CRON job.
Incident responseA CloudWatch alarm or an EventBridge event triggers an automatic action.

4.3.1 Example: Serverless Thumbnail Creation

4.4 Lambda Function URLs

  • A function URL is a dedicated HTTPS endpoint for a single Lambda function, with no API Gateway in front.
  • You protect it with IAM authentication, or you make it public and handle the authentication in the code.
  • Use API Gateway instead when you need features such as request validation, usage plans, API keys, or caching.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A Lambda function processes S3 upload events asynchronously. Some events fail every time because of bad files, and the team must keep these events for later investigation. What should a solutions architect configure?

  • A. A function URL.
  • B. A larger timeout for the function.
  • C. Provisioned concurrency.
  • D. An on-failure destination or a dead-letter queue for the function.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: D. After the retries of an asynchronous invocation, Lambda sends the failed event to a dead-letter queue or an on-failure destination, where it can be investigated.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectA function URL is a synchronous HTTPS endpoint.
BIncorrectA bad file fails no matter how long the function runs.
CIncorrectProvisioned concurrency reduces cold starts, not failures.
DCorrectThis keeps the failed events.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • API Gateway and ALB invoke Lambda synchronously. S3, SNS, and EventBridge invoke it asynchronously. SQS, Kinesis, and DynamoDB Streams use an event source mapping.
  • Asynchronous: 2 retries, then a DLQ or destination. Throttles and system errors are retried for up to 6 hours.
  • Synchronous throttling returns 429 to the caller, which must retry.

Memory Hook

Sync waits, async queues and retries twice, mappings poll.

5. Concurrency, Scaling, and Performance

Problem Statement

During a FlashCart flash sale, the order function scales up so fast that it uses all the concurrency of the Region, and the payment function is throttled. Customers also complain that the first requests after a quiet period are slow. The team needs to control the concurrency and remove the cold starts.

5.1 Concurrency

  • Concurrency is the number of requests that a function serves at the same time. Each concurrent request uses its own execution environment.
  • By default, an account has a limit of 1,000 concurrent executions across all functions in a Region, shared on demand. It can be increased to tens of thousands.
  • A useful estimate: concurrency = average requests per second × average duration in seconds. For example, 100 requests per second × 0.5 seconds = a concurrency of 50.
  • Each function can add up to 1,000 execution environments every 10 seconds.
  • When there is no concurrency left, Lambda throttles the invocations.

5.2 Reserved Concurrency

  • Reserved concurrency sets aside a number of concurrent executions for one function. No other function can use them.
  • It is also the maximum for that function, so a runaway function cannot take all the concurrency of the Region.
  • There is no charge for reserved concurrency.
  • If you do not reserve concurrency, a spike on one function, for example behind an Application Load Balancer, can throttle other functions, for example behind API Gateway.

5.3 Cold Starts and Provisioned Concurrency

  • On a cold start, Lambda must download the code and initialize the environment, so the first request has a higher latency. A large initialization, with many dependencies, takes longer.
  • Provisioned concurrency keeps a number of environments initialized in advance, so the requests that it covers have no cold start.
  • You pay for provisioned concurrency even when no request uses it. You can turn it on for expected peaks, and Application Auto Scaling can manage it on a schedule or by target utilization.
  • Remember: reserved concurrency solves throttling between functions, and provisioned concurrency solves cold starts.

5.4 Lambda SnapStart

  • SnapStart cuts the startup time, up to 10 times faster, with minimal or no code changes.
  • It is supported for Java 11 and later, Python 3.12 and later, and .NET 8 and later.
  • When you publish a version, Lambda initializes the function, takes a snapshot of the memory and disk state, and caches it. Each invocation restores the snapshot in milliseconds.
  • Avoid creating unique data during the Init phase, such as random values, UUIDs, or credentials, because every restored environment shares the snapshot.
  • The course slides describe SnapStart as having no extra cost. For Python and .NET functions, check the pricing page, because snapshot caching and restoring can be charged.

5.5 Performance Tuning

  • Increase the memory to get more CPU and network. A faster function can also cost less, because the duration is shorter.
  • Use the arm64 (Graviton) architecture for a better price and performance on many workloads.
  • Keep the package small, and initialize SDK clients outside the handler.
  • Make sure that the services behind Lambda can handle its scale. For example, API Gateway has a default throttle of 10,000 requests per second, while Lambda has a default concurrency of 1,000.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A payment function must always be able to run, even when another function in the same account has a sudden spike that uses all the concurrency of the Region. What should a solutions architect configure?

  • A. Reserved concurrency for the payment function.
  • B. Provisioned concurrency for the other function.
  • C. A larger memory size for the payment function.
  • D. SnapStart for the payment function.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: A. Reserved concurrency sets aside concurrency that no other function can use, so the payment function is not throttled by the spike.

OptionResultReason
ACorrectIt guarantees concurrency for the payment function.
BIncorrectProvisioned concurrency reduces cold starts; it does not protect other functions.
CIncorrectMemory does not reserve concurrency.
DIncorrectSnapStart reduces startup time, not throttling.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • Reserved concurrency = guarantee and limit, no cost, solves throttling. Provisioned concurrency = pre-initialized, you pay for it, solves cold starts.
  • SnapStart also reduces cold starts, for Java, Python, and .NET.
  • Throttled synchronous calls get 429. Throttled asynchronous events are retried for up to 6 hours.

Memory Hook

Reserved stops the noisy neighbor. Provisioned stops the cold start.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "One function must never be starved by another"
→ Reserved concurrency

Trigger 2: "Limit a function so it cannot overload a database"
→ Reserved concurrency as a maximum

Trigger 3: "Remove cold starts for a latency-sensitive API"
→ Provisioned concurrency

Trigger 4: "Faster startup for Java, Python, or .NET with little change"
→ Lambda SnapStart

Trigger 5: "Function needs more CPU"
→ More memory

6. Security, Networking, and Monitoring

Problem Statement

The FlashCart order function must read customer data from an RDS database in a private subnet, call an external payment API on the internet, and use database credentials without putting them in the code. The security team also asks how they will see errors and slow calls.

6.1 Permissions

  • The execution role is an IAM role that the function assumes. It grants the function access to other AWS services, such as reading from DynamoDB or writing logs.
  • A resource-based policy on the function grants other services or accounts permission to invoke it, such as S3, SNS, or API Gateway.
  • Follow least privilege: give each function its own role with only the actions it needs.
  • Store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, not in plain environment variables. Environment variables are encrypted at rest with AWS KMS.

6.2 Lambda and Your VPC

  • By default, a Lambda function runs outside your VPC, in a VPC owned by AWS. It can reach the internet and public AWS endpoints, but not the private resources in your VPC, such as an RDS database, ElastiCache, or an internal load balancer.
  • To reach private resources, you attach the function to your VPC: you choose the VPC, the subnets, and the security groups. Lambda creates an elastic network interface (ENI) in your subnets.
  • All the VPC controls apply to the ENI: security groups, route tables, and network ACLs.
  • High availability: outside a VPC, Lambda runs your function in several Availability Zones, so it keeps working if one zone has a problem. A function attached to a VPC runs only in the subnets that you choose, so attach it to subnets in at least two Availability Zones.
  • Give the subnets enough free IP addresses for the ENIs, and make sure that each zone has the routes it needs, such as a NAT gateway in each zone for internet access.
  • A function attached to a VPC has no internet access by default. To reach the internet, use private subnets with a route to a NAT gateway. To reach AWS services privately, use VPC endpoints.

6.3 Lambda With RDS Proxy

  • Many concurrent Lambda functions can open too many connections to a relational database under a high load.
  • RDS Proxy pools and shares the database connections, which improves scalability.
  • It improves availability by reducing the failover time by up to 66 percent and by preserving the connections.
  • It improves security by enforcing IAM authentication and by keeping the credentials in Secrets Manager.
  • The function must be attached to your VPC, because RDS Proxy is never publicly accessible.

6.4 Lambda With Amazon EFS

A Lambda function has no persistent disk of its own. The following table compares the places where a function can keep files:

OptionPersistent?Shared?SizeUse it for
/tmp directoryNo. It lives only as long as the execution environment.No. Each environment has its own.512 MB to 10,240 MB.Temporary files during an invocation.
LayersRead-only, part of the deployment.Yes, as code shared by functions.Within the 250 MB unzipped package limit.Libraries and shared code.
Amazon S3Yes.Yes.Virtually unlimited.Objects that the code reads and writes through the S3 API.
Amazon EFSYes.Yes, by many functions, EC2 instances, and containers at the same time.Grows and shrinks automatically.Large or shared files in directories, such as models, libraries, and data that outlive an invocation.
  • You can configure a function to mount an Amazon EFS file system to a local directory. The local mount path must start with /mnt/, for example /mnt/data.
  • The function connects to the file system over the local network in a VPC, so the function must be connected to the VPC.
  • Create the file system with a mount target in every Availability Zone that the function connects to.
  • The function uses an EFS access point. The access point connects each instance of the function to the right mount target for its Availability Zone, and it can set the user and group for the files.
  • Allow NFS traffic on port 2049 in the security groups of the function and of the mount targets.
  • If the file system has no IAM policy of its own, EFS uses a default policy that grants full access to any client that can connect through a mount target. Add a file system policy, and give the execution role only the EFS permissions it needs.
  • A function can also mount an EFS file system in another AWS account, if the security group of the file system allows inbound access from the security group of the function.
  • Many concurrent functions can put a heavy load on the file system, so choose the EFS performance and throughput settings for the workload.

6.5 Monitoring and Troubleshooting

  • Lambda sends the function logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs automatically, if the execution role allows it.
  • CloudWatch metrics include invocations, errors, duration, throttles, and concurrent executions.
  • AWS X-Ray traces a request across Lambda and the services that it calls, to find slow steps.
  • AWS CloudTrail records the management API calls on your functions, such as who changed a configuration.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A Lambda function attached to a VPC reads from an RDS database in a private subnet. It must also call a public third-party API on the internet, but the calls time out. What should a solutions architect do?

  • A. Add an internet gateway route to the private subnets.
  • B. Assign a public IP address to the function.
  • C. Detach the function from the VPC.
  • D. Place the function in private subnets that route to a NAT gateway in a public subnet.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: D. A function in a VPC has no internet access by default. A NAT gateway gives the private subnets outbound internet access while the function keeps its access to the database.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectA route to an internet gateway does not work without public IPs, and it makes the subnet public.
BIncorrectLambda ENIs do not get public IP addresses.
CIncorrectThen the function could not reach the private database.
DCorrectThis is the standard pattern for a Lambda in a VPC that needs the internet.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • A Lambda function in a VPC loses internet access. Use a NAT gateway for the internet, and VPC endpoints for AWS services.
  • Execution role = what the function can do. Resource-based policy = who can invoke the function.
  • A VPC-attached function is only as available as its subnets: choose at least two Availability Zones.
  • Too many database connections from Lambda = RDS Proxy.
  • /tmp is not shared and not persistent. Large or shared files that must outlive an invocation = EFS, which needs the function in a VPC, a mount target in each Availability Zone, and NFS port 2049 open.

Memory Hook

Role to act, policy to be invoked, NAT to go out, Proxy to share connections.

Trigger 2: "Lambda in a VPC needs the internet"

Trigger 3: "VPC-attached function must survive the loss of an Availability Zone"
→ Attach it to subnets in at least two Availability Zones

Trigger 4: "Lambda opens too many database connections"
→ Amazon RDS Proxy

Trigger 5: "Store database passwords for a function"
→ AWS Secrets Manager

Trigger 6: "Trace slow calls across services"
→ AWS X-Ray

Trigger 7: "Lambda needs large or shared files that persist between invocations"
→ Mount an Amazon EFS file system

Trigger 8: "Temporary scratch space during one invocation"
→ The /tmp directory

7. Edge Functions and Newer Options

Problem Statement

FlashCart wants to add security headers and redirect users by country at the CloudFront edge, and it also has an order workflow that must wait hours for a warehouse confirmation. The team asks which Lambda-related options fit these needs.

7.1 Code at the Edge

  • An edge function is code that you attach to a CloudFront distribution. It runs close to your users to reduce latency.
  • Uses include website security and privacy headers, dynamic web applications at the edge, search engine optimization, routing across origins and data centers, bot mitigation, real-time image transformation, A/B testing, user authentication, and user tracking.
CloudFront FunctionsLambda@Edge
RuntimeJavaScript.Node.js and Python.
ScaleMillions of requests per second.Thousands of requests per second.
TriggersViewer request and viewer response.Viewer request and response, and origin request and response.
Execution timeLess than 1 ms.5 to 10 seconds.
Memory and package2 MB of memory, 10 KB package.128 MB up to 10 GB of memory, 1 MB to 50 MB package.
Network and file system accessNo.Yes.
PricingFree tier, about one-sixth of the price of Lambda@Edge.No free tier, charged per request and duration.
Use it forCache key normalization, header changes, URL redirects and rewrites, and token validation.Longer logic, calls to other services, access to the request body, and third-party libraries.

The values in this table come from the course slides. Check the CloudFront documentation for the current limits.

7.2 Lambda@Edge in Detail

  • Lambda@Edge functions are Lambda functions, written in Node.js or Python, that scale to thousands of requests per second at the CloudFront edge.
  • You author the function in one AWS Region, US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1. CloudFront then replicates it to its edge locations around the world.
  • You associate a numbered version of the function with the CloudFront distribution, not $LATEST.
  • Lambda@Edge can change CloudFront requests and responses at four points, called triggers.
TriggerWhen it runsExample use
Viewer requestAfter CloudFront receives a request from a viewer, before it checks the cache.Authentication, URL rewrites, and redirects by country.
Origin requestBefore CloudFront forwards the request to the origin, so only on a cache miss.Choosing an origin, and A/B testing.
Origin responseAfter CloudFront receives the response from the origin, before it caches the response.Changing the response before it is cached.
Viewer responseBefore CloudFront returns the response to the viewer.Adding security headers.

Lambda@Edge does not support every Lambda feature:

  • It cannot access resources inside a VPC.
  • It does not support Lambda environment variables, except the reserved ones that Lambda sets automatically.
  • It does not support Lambda layers.
  • For viewer request events, the request body is truncated at 40 KB.
  • A function on the viewer response event cannot change the HTTP status code of the response.

7.3 Newer Lambda Options

  • Lambda durable functions run long, multi-step executions that checkpoint their progress and can wait for callbacks, such as an approval, without paying for the waiting time.
  • Lambda Managed Instances run Lambda functions on managed EC2 capacity. Asynchronous and event source mapping invocations on Managed Instances can run up to 90 minutes.
  • Lambda MicroVMs run code for up to 8 hours per execution, on the arm64 architecture.
  • Lambda Web Functions run web applications and API backends as serverless HTTP servers.
  • These options are new. The SAA-C03 exam focuses on standard Lambda functions, so learn the core limits first.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A company must add security headers to every response of its CloudFront distribution, at very high scale and the lowest cost. The logic is a few lines of JavaScript with no network calls. Which option fits best?

  • A. Lambda@Edge on the origin response.
  • B. CloudFront Functions on the viewer response.
  • C. A Lambda function behind API Gateway.
  • D. An EC2 instance in each Region.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: B. CloudFront Functions are built for lightweight, high-scale header changes at the edge, at a lower price than Lambda@Edge.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectIt works, but it is more expensive and not needed for simple header changes.
BCorrectLightweight JavaScript at the viewer level, at millions of requests per second.
CIncorrectThis does not run at the edge for every response.
DIncorrectServers add cost and management.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • CloudFront Functions = JavaScript, viewer triggers only, sub-millisecond, cheapest. Lambda@Edge = Node.js or Python, origin triggers too, network access, longer logic.
  • Lambda@Edge functions are created in us-east-1 and replicated by CloudFront. They have no VPC access, no environment variables, and no layers.
  • The origin request and origin response triggers run only when CloudFront goes to the origin, on a cache miss.

Memory Hook

Tiny and fast at the viewer: CloudFront Functions. Heavier and smarter: Lambda@Edge.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Lightweight header changes or redirects at the edge"
→ CloudFront Functions

Trigger 2: "Edge logic that calls other services or reads the body"
→ Lambda@Edge

Trigger 3: "Change the request only when CloudFront goes to the origin"
→ Lambda@Edge origin request trigger

Trigger 4: "Region where you create a Lambda@Edge function"
→ US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1

Trigger 5: "Workflow that waits hours for an approval"
→ Step Functions, or Lambda durable functions

8. Lambda Pricing

Problem Statement

The FlashCart finance team asks how the move to Lambda changes the bill, why the cost of the order function rose after a developer doubled its memory, and how to keep the cost down.

8.1 What You Pay For

  • Requests: a charge per million invocations.
  • Duration: a charge for the compute time, measured in GB-seconds: the memory that you configure multiplied by the run time, billed in 1 ms increments.
  • Extras: provisioned concurrency, ephemeral storage above 512 MB, data transfer, and other services that the function uses, such as CloudWatch Logs.
  • The course slides list a free tier of 1,000,000 requests and 400,000 GB-seconds of compute time per month. Check the pricing page for the current free tier.

8.2 Lowering the Cost

  • Right-size the memory: more memory costs more per millisecond, but it can shorten the run time. Test several sizes.
  • Use the arm64 (Graviton) architecture for a lower price per GB-second.
  • Shorten the run time: keep the package small, reuse connections, and avoid waiting in the function. Use Step Functions or asynchronous patterns instead of a function that waits.
  • Use provisioned concurrency only where cold starts matter, because you pay for it even when it is idle.
  • Filter the events in the event source mapping or the EventBridge rule, so the function runs only for the events it needs.
  • For steady, heavy traffic all day, compare the cost with containers or EC2.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A company runs a Lambda function with steady, low traffic. A developer increased its memory from 512 MB to 2,048 MB, and the monthly cost went up, but the run time barely changed. What should a solutions architect recommend?

  • A. Move the function to a VPC.
  • B. Add provisioned concurrency.
  • C. Test lower memory sizes and choose the smallest one that meets the performance goal.
  • D. Increase the timeout.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: C. Duration is billed by memory multiplied by time. If more memory does not shorten the run time, it only raises the cost.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectA VPC does not lower the compute cost.
BIncorrectProvisioned concurrency adds cost.
CCorrectRight-sizing the memory lowers the GB-seconds.
DIncorrectThe timeout does not change what you are billed for.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • Lambda cost = requests + GB-seconds (memory × duration).
  • Provisioned concurrency is charged even when idle.

Memory Hook

Pay per call and per GB-second. Right-size the memory and go arm64.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Lower the Lambda cost without code changes"
→ Right-size the memory, and use arm64

Trigger 2: "Run only for the events that matter"
→ Event filtering on the source or EventBridge rule

9.4 Lesson Summary

This lesson covered the following points:

  • Serverless means no servers to manage, automatic scaling, pay for use, and built-in availability. On AWS, it includes Lambda, Fargate, API Gateway, SQS, SNS, EventBridge, Step Functions, DynamoDB, and S3.
  • Event-driven architectures decouple producers from consumers through routers such as EventBridge, SNS, and SQS, so each part scales and fails on its own. Step Functions orchestrates ordered steps.
  • Lambda runs stateless functions for up to 15 minutes, with 128 MB to 10,240 MB of memory, and CPU that grows with memory. It runs from .zip archives or container images, with layers, versions, and aliases.
  • Lambda is invoked synchronously, asynchronously (2 retries, then a DLQ or destination), or through event source mappings.
  • Concurrency is 1,000 per Region by default. Reserved concurrency guarantees and limits a function, and provisioned concurrency and SnapStart reduce cold starts.
  • A function in a VPC uses an ENI, needs a NAT gateway for the internet, should use RDS Proxy for relational databases, and can mount Amazon EFS for persistent, shared files. You pay for requests and GB-seconds.

Memory Hook

Events in, functions run, pay per use: and know the 15-minute, 10 GB, and 1,000 numbers.

10. Knowledge Check

Answer each question in your own words before you open the model answer.

Question 1: Explain what serverless means and give three AWS serverless services.

Maps to: Objectives 1 and 2 (Comprehension).

Serverless means that you do not provision, patch, or manage servers. The service scales automatically, you pay for what you use, and availability is built in. Servers still exist, but AWS manages them. AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, Amazon EventBridge, AWS Step Functions, and AWS Fargate are serverless services.

Question 2: Compare synchronous and asynchronous communication, and explain how an event-driven architecture improves resilience.

Maps to: Objective 2 (Analysis).

In synchronous communication, the caller waits for the answer, so a slow or failed receiver slows or breaks the caller. In asynchronous communication, the caller sends a message and moves on. An event-driven architecture has producers that publish events, a router such as EventBridge or SNS, and consumers that react. The producers do not depend on the consumers, so each part scales and fails independently, queues absorb spikes, and new consumers can be added without changing the producers.

Question 3: Describe the Lambda execution environment, the cold start, and the main limits of a function.

Maps to: Objective 3 (Comprehension).

Lambda runs each function in an isolated execution environment. The Init phase downloads the code, starts the runtime, and runs the code outside the handler, and the Invoke phase runs the handler for each event. A cold start includes the Init phase, and warm environments are reused. A function can use 128 MB to 10,240 MB of memory, with CPU in proportion, can run up to 15 minutes, has 4 KB of environment variables, up to 5 layers, a 250 MB unzipped package or a 10 GB container image, and accounts have 1,000 concurrent executions per Region by default.

Question 4: Compare the three ways to invoke Lambda, and explain how errors are handled for asynchronous invocations.

Maps to: Objective 4 (Application).

Synchronous invocation, from API Gateway, an ALB, a function URL, or the SDK, makes the caller wait for the result, and the caller handles errors and 429 throttles. Asynchronous invocation, from S3, SNS, or EventBridge, queues the event and returns at once. Lambda retries a function error 2 more times, retries throttles and system errors for up to 6 hours, and then sends the event to a dead-letter queue or an on-failure destination. Event source mappings poll SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams, and MSK and invoke the function with batches.

Question 5: Explain the difference between reserved concurrency, provisioned concurrency, and SnapStart.

Maps to: Objective 5 (Analysis).

Reserved concurrency sets aside concurrency for one function and caps it, at no cost, so other functions cannot starve it and it cannot overload a downstream system. Provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialized in advance to remove cold starts, and you pay for it even when idle. SnapStart restores a snapshot of an initialized environment to cut the startup time, for Java, Python, and .NET.

Question 6: Explain how a Lambda function reaches a private RDS database and the internet, and why RDS Proxy helps.

Maps to: Objective 6 (Application).

You attach the function to your VPC by choosing subnets and security groups, and Lambda creates an ENI in the subnets. The function then reaches private resources, but it loses internet access, so you route the private subnets to a NAT gateway, and use VPC endpoints for AWS services. Many concurrent functions can open too many database connections, so RDS Proxy pools and shares them, shortens failover, and uses IAM authentication with credentials in Secrets Manager.

Question 7: Design a serverless order system for FlashCart that handles flash-sale spikes, protects the payment function, has no cold starts on the API, and keeps failed events.

Maps to: Objective 7 (Synthesis).

Use API Gateway with a Lambda order function that writes the order to an SQS queue or publishes an "order placed" event to EventBridge, so the spike is absorbed and the payment, email, and analytics consumers scale independently. Give the payment function reserved concurrency so it is never starved, and the API function provisioned concurrency or SnapStart for low latency. Configure dead-letter queues or on-failure destinations for the asynchronous consumers. Use RDS Proxy if the functions use a relational database, CloudWatch and X-Ray for monitoring, and right-size the memory, with arm64, to control the cost.

Question 8: Explain the storage options of a Lambda function, and how to give several functions access to the same persistent files.

Maps to: Objective 6 (Application).

The /tmp directory is temporary and belongs to one execution environment, layers are read-only shared code, and S3 stores objects through its API. For files that must persist and be shared, mount an Amazon EFS file system: connect the function to the VPC, create a mount target in every Availability Zone that the function uses, allow NFS traffic on port 2049 in the security groups, and mount the file system through an EFS access point at a path that starts with /mnt/. Protect it with a file system policy and least-privilege permissions in the execution role.
